title: Evaluation of oxidative stress biomarkers in urine of type 2 diabetes patients
author: Kurutas, Gumusalan, et al.
materials: 20 patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), 20 patients with diabetic nephropathy (DN) and 14 healthy individuals as control were involved in this study. Timed first morning urine samples were taken from patients and healthy groups on the zero, 1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, 15th and 30th days. Index of individuality and reference change value were calculated from within-subject and between-subject variations. Methods of oxidative stress biomarkers in human blood were adopted in human urine and markers were measured as spectrophotometrically. Also, analytical quality specifications for evaluation of the method performance were established for oxidative stress biomarkers in urine.

steps.title: Collect timed urine samples
steps.instruction: Collect first‑morning urine from 20 type‑2 diabetes (T2DM) patients, 20 diabetic nephropathy (DN) patients, and 14 healthy controls on days 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 15, and 30 (seven samples per individual).

steps.title: Measure biomarkers spectrophotometrically
steps.instruction: Apply the oxidative‑stress biomarker methods originally developed for human blood to each urine sample and record the spectrophotometric absorbance values for all analytes.

steps.title: Log‑transform data and remove outliers
steps.instruction: Transform all biomarker concentrations to natural logarithms. Test duplicate measurements for outliers using the Cochran test, then apply the Reed test. Exclude the identified outliers: five T2DM samples (all analytes) and two healthy‑individual MDA samples from the Cochran test, and one healthy‑individual MDA sample from the Reed test.

steps.title: Compute analytical variance and CVA
steps.instruction: For each analyte, calculate analytical variance using SDA² = Σd² / (2n), where d is the difference between duplicate measurements and n is the number of duplicate pairs. Express SDA² as a relative SDA to the first sample concentration to obtain the analytical coefficient of variation (CVA).

steps.title: Separate biological and analytical variance
steps.instruction: Perform one‑way ANOVA to obtain between‑subject variance (SDG²) and total within‑subject variance (SDTI²). Compute the within‑subject biological variance as SDI² = SDTI² – SDA².

steps.title: Calculate Index of Individuality
steps.instruction: Calculate within‑subject coefficient of variation (CVI) and between‑subject coefficient of variation (CVG) using each individual’s homeostatic mean and the overall mean, respectively. Compute the Index of Individuality (II) as II = CVI / CVG; note that II < 1.40 indicates low individuality (high usefulness of population‑based reference intervals).

steps.title: Calculate Reference Change Value
steps.instruction: Use Z = 1.96 (95 % bidirectional). Compute RCV = √2 × Z × √(CVA² + CVI²), which simplifies to RCV = 2.77 × CVTI.

steps.title: Derive quality specifications
steps.instruction: Calculate the desirable analytical quality specifications: I = 0.5 × CVI; B = 0.25 × √(CVI² + CVG²); TE = 1.65 × (0.25 × CVI) + 0.25 × √(CVI² + CVG²).

steps.title: Conduct statistical tests
steps.instruction: Compare mean within‑subject variances between groups (DN vs healthy, T2DM vs healthy, DN vs T2DM) using the F test. Assess time‑dependent trends for CAT, CuZnSOD, and MDA with linear regression. Perform group comparisons (e.g., male vs female, disease status) using the Mann–Whitney U test. Consider p < 0.05 statistically significant.
